subtype_label: Focus internal / focus inference (no given focus)
query: Help me understand what's worth attention in these goal records.

judge.implied_focus: Goal health / at-risk goals worth attention (goals that are underperforming, stalled, or anomalous relative to their targets)

per_column.name: completion_gap
per_column.rationale: Quantifies shortfall between target and actual progress; a direct measure of which goals are lagging and deserve attention.

per_column.name: target_achievement_ratio
per_column.rationale: Normalized attainment metric complementing the raw gap; distinguishes over- vs under-achievers, reinforcing the performance-risk focus.

per_column.name: priority_rigor
per_column.rationale: Escalation-style classification (routine/medium/high concern/delayed_high_priority) that flags which goals warrant scrutiny, tying priority to concern level.

per_column.name: anomaly_flag
per_column.rationale: Explicitly encodes problem types (date_anomaly, stalled_goal, high_target_low_progress, critical_cancelled); the clearest realization of 'what's worth attention'.

judge.rationale: All four columns converge on a single coherent, data-inferable focus: identifying goals that are at risk or otherwise noteworthy. Two continuous performance measures (completion_gap, target_achievement_ratio) provide graded severity, while two categorical classifiers (priority_rigor, anomaly_flag) surface discrete concern types. This forms a sound multi-facet analytical structure — severity magnitude plus qualitative flags — at a useful granularity rather than a single restatement or generic noise. The focus is highly actionable: an analyst can triage stalled/high_target_low_progress/critical_cancelled goals and prioritize investigation. Minor deduction on structure because achievement_ratio and completion_gap are partially redundant (both target-vs-progress), and 'routine' dominates priority_rigor, slightly limiting its discriminating power.
